    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Having uprooted all relationships with his sister because of intense selfishness, Kaṁsa, who was sitting on his knees, grasped the newborn child by the legs and tried to dash her against the surface of a stone.
    Commentary

    He threw the child down with great force (apothayet).

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    This verse shows his cruel nature. Jāta-mātrāṁ means the new born child which was still wet with embryonic fluids. Hari-vaṁśa says sā garbha-śayana-kliṣṭā garbhāklinnamūrddhaja: the child, in pain from being in the womb, had its head moist with fluid.

    Related values & verses
    Related values
    Dana (Charity / Generosity)Anahankarah (Freedom from False Ego)Tyaga (Renunciation / Letting Go)Discriminative Wisdom
    Related verses
    SB 10.4.5 SB 10.4.6 SB 10.4.7 SB 10.4.9 SB 10.4.10 BG 3.30 BG 14.1 BG 15.2 BG 15.9 BG 6.4 BG 18.64
    Personal Guidance
    When sva-artha (selfishness) uproots sauhṛda (affection), even kinship becomes prey — guard the heart from the ahaṅkāra that turns love into use.
    Practical Applications
    • Notice one relationship today where you have quietly reduced a person to their utility for you, and restore them to soul-status in your speech.
    • Refuse to act on a self-serving impulse when it would override a bond of trust — pause, name the sva-artha, and offer the moment to Kṛṣṇa.
    • Speak to a family member today with no agenda, no ask, no leverage — practice sauhṛda untainted by what you want from them.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where in my life have I, like Kaṁsa, allowed sva-artha (selfish interest) to silently uproot a sauhṛda — a bond of natural affection — and called it pragmatism?
    • What 'newborn' good in me — a fresh impulse toward bhakti, a tender resolution, a vulnerable relationship — am I about to dash against the stone of self-preservation, and what fear is driving the hand?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • Notice the next time a friendship in your class or hostel cools right when your interests diverged — a different stream, a different friend group, a competing crush — and ask honestly: was it really 'we grew apart,' or did svārtha quietly uproot sauhṛda?
    • Before you post, repost, or pile-on online today, pause and check: am I about to harm someone's reputation because their existence threatens my self-image, my grades-ranking, my social standing? That is the Kaṁsa-impulse in miniature — the seed of svārtha-unmūlita. Step back.
    • Pick one person whose presence makes you feel smaller — a topper, a more popular classmate, a sibling who gets more attention — and do one concrete act of genuine support for them this week. Watch how strongly the ahaṅkāra resists. That resistance is the verse, lit up inside you.
    householder
    • In the next family financial decision — a property, an inheritance, a school choice, an aging parent's care — write down the option that is best for your soul-bond with these people, and the option that is best for your svārtha. If they differ, that gap is exactly the territory this verse is warning you about.
    • When you catch yourself rehearsing a 'reasonable' argument for why a sibling, in-law, or co-parent should accept a decision that mostly benefits you, name it inwardly as svārtha before you speak it aloud. Often, just naming it dissolves the need to win.
    • Once a week, perform one act of seva for your spouse or child that has zero strategic return — not to be remembered, not to be repaid, not even to be noticed. This rebuilds sauhṛda on a non-svārtha foundation while there is still time.
    senior
    • Examine your will, your assets, and your stated wishes: is anything there shaped by a quiet desire to keep being important after you are gone — to hold a child, a temple, an institution on a leash? Loosen one such grip this month as a deliberate act of tyāga.
    • When mentoring a younger person — child, grandchild, junior colleague — notice if you are subtly steering them toward decisions that protect your legacy rather than serve their soul. Real compassion at this stage is for their svadharma, not for your self-continuation.
    • Sit each evening with the recognition that the body you have transitioned through is nearing its final passage, and that nothing svārtha-built will cross with you. Use that clarity to forgive one old grievance where you were 'wronged' — most of those wounds, examined now, were two svārthas colliding, not soul against soul.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Reading this verse as a cautionary tale about 'other people like Kaṁsa' rather than recognizing the same svārtha-driven calculus operating, in subtler form, in one's own decisions today.
    • Mistaking Kaṁsa's failure as merely ethical (he was cruel) and missing the deeper diagnosis — that ahaṅkāra fused to self-interest will sever even the most natural bonds, so the cure is anāhaṅkāra, not better ethics.
    • Using the call to vairāgya and tyāga as cover for cutting off relationships and duties one finds inconvenient — Kaṁsa-style 'detachment' from sauhṛda dressed up as renunciation, when real vairāgya is detachment from viṣaya, not from one's responsibilities to others.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Kaṁsa's sauhṛda (affection) for his sister was 'uprooted' the moment her child threatened his position. Where in your own life have you felt affection quietly disappear the moment self-interest was at stake — and did you admit it was happening, or did you rename it 'being practical'?
    • The verse calls Kaṁsa's act svārtha-unmūlita — selfishness as a tree-pulling force. We tend to picture selfishness as small (a stingy moment, a white lie). What is the most 'reasonable-sounding' selfishness you have witnessed in a respected person — family, boss, leader — that, traced to its root, would tear up relationships if pursued? Disagree with each other on where the line sits.
    • If real compassion is for the soul and material compassion is for the body, then Kaṁsa's failure was not just cruelty — it was a total inversion of values. Discuss: is it possible to be a 'good' family man, dutiful employee, kind neighbour, and still be living a Kaṁsa-logic of self-preservation at the level of the soul? Push back on each other; do not let the group settle on a comfortable answer.
    Role Play

    Two students play siblings who jointly inherit a modest family home. Sibling A (the 'Kaṁsa seat') has just been told by a financial advisor that selling the home immediately, against the dying wish of their father, will secure A's career and lifestyle for the next decade. Sibling B wants to keep the home as a place for the extended family, including A's own children, to gather. A must argue for the sale — using only language that sounds reasonable, responsible, even loving ('I am doing this for the family's future'). B must listen and then name, without insulting, the exact moment svārtha begins to uproot sauhṛda in A's reasoning. A third student observes and reports back where the group itself was tempted to side with A's 'sensible' framing. Then swap roles.

    Objections & Responses
    • This verse is just a horror story about an ancient tyrant. What does an infanticidal king have to do with my life? I am not Kaṁsa.
      Gauḍīya teachers read these śāstric portraits as mirrors, not museum pieces. Kaṁsa is not a one-off villain; he is the logical end-point of a principle we all carry — svārtha that, when threatened, will quietly dissolve every bond it once cherished. Most of us never reach the stone-slab; we reach only the small betrayals — the friend dropped when inconvenient, the parent visited less when promotion came, the truth softened to protect a position. The verse is precisely meant to startle us before we drift further down that line. To say 'I am not Kaṁsa' is exactly what Kaṁsa would have said the day before his sister's wedding.
    • Telling people to suspect their own affection as secret selfishness will just make them anxious and cynical. Healthy relationships need trust in our own love, not constant suspicion of it.
      Gauḍīya sādhana does not ask you to distrust love; it asks you to locate it correctly. Sauhṛda built only on shared svārtha is fragile — it will, as in Kaṁsa's case, snap the instant interests diverge. Sauhṛda anchored in seeing Kṛṣṇa in the other — the same eternal soul the Gītā describes in 2.13 — only deepens under pressure, because its root is not in what the other gives me. So the practice is not anxious self-suspicion; it is vairāgya from svārtha as the load-bearing wall of relationship, and the steady transfer of that weight onto bhakti. The result is not less affection but affection that no longer needs to be defended at someone else's expense.

    The child, Yoga-māyā-devī, the younger sister of Lord Viṣṇu, slipped upward from Kaṁsa’s hands and appeared in the sky as Devī, the goddess Durgā, with eight arms, completely equipped with weapons.
    Purport

    Kaṁsa tried to dash the child downward against a piece of stone, but since she was Yoga-māyā, the younger sister of Lord Viṣṇu, she slipped upward and assumed the form of the goddess Durgā. The word anujā, meaning “the younger sister,” is significant. When Viṣṇu, or Kṛṣṇa, took birth from Devakī, He must have simultaneously taken birth from Yaśodā also. Otherwise how could Yoga-māyā have been anujā, the Lord’s younger sister?

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    The child, Yogamāyā-devī, the younger sister of Lord Viṣṇu, slipped upward from Kaṁsa's hands and appeared in the sky as Devī, the goddess Durgā, with eight arms, completely equipped with weapons.
    Commentary

    10. 11. As she was falling to the ground, Mayadevi then with great force leaped up into the sky. Bhaviysa uttara Purana says that she put her foot on his head as she went up into the sky. She is described here as the younger sister of Krsna or Visnu, indicating that Krsna as well as Maya was born from Yasoda. She held weapons in her eight arms to frighten Kamsa.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Though thrown down, she sudden rose up. Bhaviśyottara says kaṁsāsurasyottamāṅge pādaṁ dattvā gatā divam: putting her feet on Kaṁsa’s head she rose in the sky. Her celestial form (devī) was seen by Kaṁsa and others in order to give him faith in her words. She showed a large form with many hands to frighten him. Kṛṣṇa is called Viṣṇu, pervading everywhere, because he entered the minds of Devakī and Yaśodā simultaneously. She is called the younger sister, because she was born from Yaśodā after Kṛṣṇa entered Yaśodā’s mind. Of course Devakī identified the girl as her own out of affection for Yaśodā and thus she regarded her as Kṛṣṇa’s younger sister.

    Related values & verses

    Personal Guidance
    Yoga-māyā, Kṛṣṇa's anujā, slips Kaṁsa's grip and reveals herself as Durgā — the Lord's potency shields His descent and humbles every would-be tyrant.
    Practical Applications
    • Notice today where you are playing 'Kaṁsa' — trying to crush an outcome by force — and consciously hand that grip over to Kṛṣṇa's arrangement.
    • When a plan slips out of your hands unexpectedly, refuse the panic-reading and ask instead what Yoga-māyā may be protecting on Kṛṣṇa's behalf.
    • Offer one praṇāma to Yoga-māyā-devī before sādhana, asking her to remove the false ego that keeps you from seeing Kṛṣṇa as the Personality behind every event.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where in my life am I treating Kṛṣṇa's protective arrangements as mere coincidence, missing the hand of Yoga-māyā at work in moments I escaped harm I did not deserve to escape?
    • When have I, like Kaṁsa, tried to crush something I feared — only to discover the very thing I struck at was not what I thought it was, and what is the envy in me that still wants to strike?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • When an exam result, a college admit, or a 'situationship' feels like Kaṁsa's hand closing on your future — pause before the panic-scroll. Name out loud: 'this outcome is in Yoga-māyā's hands, not the algorithm's, not my crush's, not the admissions officer's.' Then do the next concrete piece of sva-dharma: open the book, send the honest message, sleep.
    • Audit your social-media feed this week as a viṣaya diet. Whose 'eight-armed' highlight reel are you mistaking for the real Devī, and worshipping for material boons (validation, comparison wins, FOMO relief)? Unfollow three accounts that feed the ahaṅkāra and replace them with one that points to Kṛṣṇa.
    • When a friend group pressures you toward something your conscience flags — cheating on an assignment, mocking someone, a substance, a relationship line — remember Kaṁsa heard Devī's warning and still acted from ego. Practice one small, awkward act of standing apart this week, and write down afterward what it cost the false ego (not what it cost socially).
    householder
    • In family decisions — the school for the child, the job offer, the move, the investment — explicitly distinguish material compassion (keeping everyone bodily comfortable, conflict-free) from real compassion (serving each soul's progress toward Kṛṣṇa). Make one decision this month where you choose the second even when the first lobbies hard.
    • Money, career outcomes, and your children's trajectories are the 'infants' you most want to control with a Kaṁsa-grip. Each Sunday evening with your spouse, name aloud the three outcomes you have been clutching, and formally hand them back to Yoga-māyā — then plan only the next week's dharma, not the decade's results.
    • Raise your children to know Kṛṣṇa is the supreme Personality, not an impersonal 'energy' or one deity among many. This week, tell them the SB 10.4.9 pastime in your own words at dinner — Kaṁsa's hand, Devī slipping upward, the warning he ignored — and ask them where in their school week they saw a 'Kaṁsa moment.'
    senior
    • Mortality is the one outcome the Kaṁsa in all of us has been gripping hardest. Sit each morning with the fact that Yoga-māyā, not your planning, governs the hour of departure — and use that clarity to simplify one attachment this week (a possession, a grudge, a role you are still performing).
    • Your legacy is not your estate, your reputation, or even your children's worldly success — those are the boons Kaṁsa wanted from Devī. Identify one younger person (child, grandchild, neighbor, mentee) and this month transmit one specific thing from the paramparā to them: a verse, a pastime, a habit of sādhana. Make it concrete, not 'be a good person.'
    • Loosen your grip the way Kaṁsa would not. Pick one āśrama-appropriate renunciation this season — a committee you chair, a financial decision you still control, a household opinion you still enforce — and quietly hand it to the next generation, then use the freed time for extra japa, śravaṇam, and association of devotees.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Reducing Yoga-māyā to a symbolic 'feminine principle' or generic Devī archetype, severing her from her concrete identity as the anujā — the younger sister of Viṣṇu — and thereby slipping into impersonalist abstraction.
    • Confusing Yoga-māyā (Kṛṣṇa's internal potency who arranges His pastimes) with mahā-māyā (the external illusory energy that binds conditioned souls), and so misreading every appearance of 'Durgā' as the same energy.
    • Taking the verse as a cinematic miracle to admire from a distance, rather than as evidence that surrender to Kṛṣṇa is met by real, personal protection — and therefore failing to actually surrender today's fear into His hands.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Yoga-māyā slips upward from Kaṁsa's grip and reveals herself as the eight-armed Devī. Share with your partner: where in your own life is a 'Kaṁsa-grip' currently trying to crush something — and where, on honest reflection, has Kṛṣṇa's internal potency already slipped it free without you noticing? Press each other if the answer sounds rehearsed.
    • Prabhupāda underlines anujā — the younger sister — and insists Yoga-māyā must have simultaneously taken birth from Yaśodā. Discuss: does this kind of literal, structural reading of a 'mythological' detail strengthen your śraddhā or strain it? Be honest about where you push back. Don't let the group settle on a polite consensus.
    • Kaṁsa sees Devī armed with eight weapons and still does not surrender. In pairs, name one warning the Lord has already given you — through circumstance, scripture, or a person — that you, like Kaṁsa, have explained away. What is the ahaṅkāra still defending?
    Role Play

    Two students. Student A is a college roommate who has just been passed over for a coveted internship that A was sure was theirs by right; A is furious, sleepless, blaming a professor, a classmate, the system. Student B is a friend who has been studying SB 10.4.9 this week. B's task: without quoting the verse like a slogan, help A see that the 'crushing hand' A imagines holding their future is not actually in control — Yoga-māyā governs every outcome under Kṛṣṇa's will — and that real compassion is not telling A 'you'll be fine' (material consolation) but pointing A toward sva-dharma and sādhana (service to the soul). After 5 minutes, swap. Then debrief: where did B drift into generic pep talk? Where did A's ahaṅkāra resist the personalist framing?

    Objections & Responses
    • This is just mythology dressed up as theology. A baby slipping out of a king's hands and turning into an eight-armed goddess in the sky — surely a serious modern reader has to treat this as symbolic, not historical.
      A Gauḍīya teacher would not concede the dichotomy. The verse is not 'symbolic versus historical' — it is both fully real and fully meaningful. Yoga-māyā is Kṛṣṇa's internal potency; her appearing in eight-armed Devī form is precisely the kind of event that should not fit our materially-conditioned categories, because the moment it does, we have shrunk Bhagavān to fit the modern reader rather than letting the modern reader be enlarged by Bhagavān. Śraddhā does not mean switching off discrimination; it means trusting the paramparā — Vyāsa, Śukadeva, Sūta, down to Prabhupāda — over our own short experience. Try the verse on as true for a year of sādhana and watch what it does to the heart, before deciding it is metaphor.
    • If Devī Durgā is the same Yoga-māyā who is Viṣṇu's younger sister, then aren't all paths and all deities really the same? Worship Durgā, worship Viṣṇu — what's the difference?
      The verse actually says the opposite of what the syncretist hears. Anujā — 'younger sister' — is a relational word. It places Yoga-māyā in subordinate, serving relation to Viṣṇu/Kṛṣṇa; she is His potency, not His equal and not an alternative Absolute. Worshipping Durgā for material boons — wealth, protection, the removal of enemies — is exactly what Kaṁsa's whole world is built on, and it does not save him. Devī herself, in this very pastime, points away from herself to the One who has already taken birth elsewhere. The Gauḍīya line honors Devī as Kṛṣṇa's internal energy and does not flatten her into Kṛṣṇa, nor flatten Kṛṣṇa into one demigod among many. Surrender (sarva-dharmān parityajya) is to Him personally.

    The goddess Durgā was decorated with flower garlands, smeared with sandalwood pulp and dressed with excellent garments and ornaments made of valuable jewels. Holding in her hands a bow, a trident, arrows, a shield, a sword, a conchshell, a disc and a club, and being praised by celestial beings like Apsarās, Kinnaras, Uragas, Siddhas, Cāraṇas and Gandharvas, who worshiped her with all kinds of presentations, she spoke as follows.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    The goddess Durgā was decorated with flower garlands, smeared with sandalwood pulp and dressed with excellent garments and ornaments made of valuable jewels. Holding in her hands a bow, a trident, arrows, a shield, a sword, a conchshell, a disc and a club, and being praised by celestial beings like Apsarās, Kinnaras, Uragas, Siddhas, Cāraṇas and Gandharvas, who worshiped her with all kinds of presentations, she spoke as follows.
    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The list of praisers is not exhaustive.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    They offered gifts like milk and honey.

    Related values & verses
    Related values
    Anahankarah (Freedom from False Ego)Discriminative Wisdom
    Related verses
    SB 10.4.7 SB 10.4.8 SB 10.4.9 SB 10.4.12 SB 10.4.13 BG 3.30 BG 14.1 BG 15.2 BG 15.9 BG 6.4 BG 18.64
    Personal Guidance
    Even Yogamāyā, fully armed and worshiped by celestials, stands as Kṛṣṇa's servant — true power is service to Him, not self-display.
    Practical Applications
    • Notice today where you are accumulating 'weapons' — credentials, status, defenses — and ask whom they actually serve.
    • Before any task that earns you praise, silently offer it to Kṛṣṇa and refuse to claim the result as your own.
    • Speak to one person today as Yogamāyā speaks here — from a position of strength used entirely in Kṛṣṇa's service, not for yourself.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where am I, like Kaṁsa, mistaking an external 'enemy' as the source of my fear, when the real cause of my suffering is my own envy of Kṛṣṇa's supremacy?
    • Which weapons of māyā — the bow of distraction, the trident of the three guṇas, the sword of false ego — am I currently being held by, mistaking them for instruments I myself wield?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • When you see a classmate, influencer, or senior with obvious 'powers' — top grades, follower counts, social dominance — practice the discriminative wisdom this verse models: ask whose servant they are, not just what they can do. Power without that question is the Kaṁsa view.
    • Today, do one act of seva that no one will post or see — clean a shared space, message a struggling friend, help a sibling with homework — specifically because Yogamāyā's whole role is to serve unseen behind Kṛṣṇa's plan. Match her style, not the influencer's.
    • When a teacher, coach, or parent says something hard you do not want to hear, pause before reacting and ask whether your ahaṅkāra is treating their correction the way Kaṁsa treated the goddess — as a threat to be killed off rather than a message to be heard.
    householder
    • In your next significant family or work decision this week, deliberately separate real compassion from material compassion — are you protecting someone's soul-trajectory or just their bodily comfort? Name it out loud to your spouse before acting.
    • The goddess holds eight weapons but is herself a servant. Hold your professional 'weapons' — title, salary, expertise, network — the same way: as instruments of seva for your family and for Kṛṣṇa, not as identity. This week, refuse one prestige move and accept one humble service.
    • When raising your children, do not flatten Kṛṣṇa into 'a god' or 'the universe.' Speak of Him personally, by name, in the home — at meals, before sleep, when something goes wrong — so they grow up with the personalist line, not vague spirituality.
    senior
    • Review the 'weapons and ornaments' you have accumulated over a lifetime — positions held, properties owned, reputations earned — and begin, this month, to set them down deliberately, the way one prepares offerings. Pick one and release it before the next ekādaśī.
    • When younger family members come for advice, resist the temptation to give material counsel only. Speak to the soul in them, as the verse implies the soul is what is real. Mentor at least one person this season specifically on sva-dharma and bhakti, not only career.
    • Use the body's current signals — slower steps, fading senses, friends departing — as direct training in anahankarah. Each diminishment is the Lord loosening a grip you would not have loosened on your own; thank Him by name when you notice it, rather than resisting.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Treating Durgā as an independent supreme deity to be petitioned for material gains, rather than recognizing her as Kṛṣṇa's potency executing His will — sliding into demigod-confusion the verse explicitly warns against.
    • Romanticizing the imagery of garlands, jewels, and celestial worshipers as aesthetic spirituality, while missing that this opulence is the very face of māyā that binds the conditioned soul.
    • Reading the verse as mythological decoration about ancient beings (Apsarās, Kinnaras, Gandharvas) rather than recognizing that Durgā's eight weapons operate on me right now through the modes of nature.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Yogamāyā, taken as Durgā, appears with weapons, jewels, and the worship of celestial beings — yet she is the Lord's potency, not the supreme. Where in your own practice do you find yourself drawn toward the powerful agent rather than the One she serves? Share an honest example with your partner; do not let each other off the hook with abstractions.
    • Kaṁsa mistakes the small girl for an ordinary infant and tries to kill her — and is shown the cosmic Durgā instead. Discuss with your group: when has your discriminative wisdom failed in the opposite direction — dismissing as small or ordinary something that was actually the Lord's arrangement? Disagree if you must about whether such 'signs' are real or self-flattery.
    • The verse lists eight weapons in her hands and six classes of celestial beings praising her. Is this elaborate iconography essential to the verse's teaching, or could the same lesson be conveyed without it? Defend your view; do not collapse into 'it's all symbolic' or 'it's all literal.'
    Role Play

    Two students play the scene: one is Kaṁsa, who has just had the infant slip from his hands and seen the eight-armed goddess rise into the sky, praised by Gandharvas and Apsarās. The other is Kaṁsa's minister, a rationalist who insists what he saw was hallucination from stress. Kaṁsa must decide in the next two minutes whether to keep hunting newborns or to stop. The minister presses him with modern arguments (trauma, projection, political theater); Kaṁsa must respond from what he actually witnessed. After three minutes, swap roles. The teacher then asks the class: at what point did discriminative wisdom (or its absence) decide Kaṁsa's fate?

    Objections & Responses
    • This is just Hindu polytheism dressed up — a goddess with weapons, worshiped by demigods. How is this different from any other pagan pantheon, and why should a serious modern reader take it as anything but mythology?
      Notice carefully: the goddess herself does not claim supremacy here. She is Yogamāyā, Kṛṣṇa's potency, dispatched to protect the Lord's plan. The Gauḍīya line is unambiguously personalist — Kṛṣṇa alone is the supreme Personality of Godhead, and every other being, however exalted, however many-armed, however praised by Gandharvas, is His servant. The verse is not pantheon-flattening; it is hierarchy-revealing. The Apsarās, Kinnaras, Uragas, Siddhas, Cāraṇas, and Gandharvas are real classes of living entities in the cosmic structure, but they all stand under Kṛṣṇa. To read this as 'just another pagan deity' is precisely the demigod-confusion the tradition warns against.
    • If Yogamāyā is so powerful, why does she need Kṛṣṇa at all? And if Kṛṣṇa is so powerful, why does He need her to swap places with the infant in Kaṁsa's prison? The whole arrangement seems redundant.
      It is not redundant; it is the very texture of līlā. Kṛṣṇa acts through His potencies precisely so that the personal exchange of love (rasa) is preserved. If He did everything by direct fiat, there would be no devotees, no servants, no drama of bhakti. Yogamāyā's apparent independence is the Lord's own arrangement — she serves Him by appearing to act on her own. This is also why surrender is to Kṛṣṇa personally, not to the potency: she herself bows to Him. The seva displayed here — six classes of celestial beings worshiping her, and she in turn serving His plan — is the cosmos rehearsing the structure of bhakti. To call it redundant is to miss that relationship, not efficiency, is the point.

    O Kaṁsa, you fool, what will be the use of killing me? The Supreme Personality of Godhead, who has been your enemy from the very beginning and who will certainly kill you, has already taken His birth somewhere else. Therefore, do not unnecessarily kill other children.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    O Kaṁsa, you fool, what will be the use of killing me? The Supreme Personality of Godhead, who has been your enemy from the very beginning and who will certainly kill you, has already taken His birth somewhere else. Therefore, do not unnecessarily kill other children.
    Commentary

    "What can you gain from killing me? If you kill me, you still cannot prevent your own death. He who will kill you has already been born in some place, which cannot be revealed to you (yatra kva va)." Krpanam refers to Devaki who is suffering. Another reading is krpanan, in which case it refers to many poor babies. Instead of "You should not kill the poor Devaki" the sentence would read "You should not kill the poor innocent children."

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    O fool (manda)! What is the use even if you had killed me? He who will kill you has been born somewhere though I cannot clearly say the place. Therefore I will not kill you today. In a previous birth he killed you. Do not afflict poor Devakī by keeping her imprisoned. Release her along with her husband. You should also offer them some money. Instead of kṛpanām sometimes kṛpnanān is seen. Then the meaning is “Do not kill other helpless children thinking that they will kill you because they are related to the couple.”

    Related values & verses
    Related values
    Anahankarah (Freedom from False Ego)Discriminative WisdomVinaya (Humility / Modesty)
    Related verses
    SB 10.4.9 SB 10.4.10 SB 10.4.13 SB 10.4.14 SB 10.4.15 BG 3.30 BG 14.1 BG 15.2 BG 15.9 BG 6.4 BG 18.64
    Personal Guidance
    Kṛṣṇa cannot be killed by any scheme of the envious — surrender to Him, not to your own clever plans for self-protection.
    Practical Applications
    • Notice today where you are scheming to control an outcome Kṛṣṇa already governs, and drop one such maneuver before sundown.
    • Refuse to take out your fear on someone weaker — when anxiety rises, name the real source rather than wounding the kṛpaṇa nearest you.
    • Speak Kṛṣṇa's name aloud once when threatened or insulted today, trusting that the ante-kṛt of every false fear has already taken His birth.
    Reflection Questions
    • Devakī addresses Kaṁsa as 'manda' (fool) while pleading for the lives of others — where in my life have I tried to reason with a tyrannical impulse (in myself or another) by appealing to its self-interest rather than confronting it directly?
    • The verse turns on the assurance that Kṛṣṇa, the real anta-kṛt, has already been born elsewhere beyond Kaṁsa's reach — what 'kṛpaṇān' (helpless ones, including my own dependents and lower nature) am I still failing to protect because I doubt that Kṛṣṇa's arrangement is already in motion without me?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • Notice the next time you are afraid of one specific person or outcome (a rival, a rejection, a grade) and find yourself snapping at someone unrelated — a sibling, a roommate, a group chat. Name it out loud to yourself: 'I am Kaṁsa right now; this person is not my enemy.' Then apologize before bed.
    • When peer pressure pushes you to pile on someone — a classmate being mocked, a junior being hazed, a stranger being dragged on social media — refuse to add the next blow. The pile-on is exactly Kaṁsa's logic: harming the kṛpaṇa to feel safer in the group. Walk away from the thread or change the subject in person.
    • Before a high-stakes exam or interview, write down the actual thing you fear (failing, looking stupid, disappointing parents). Naming the real fear stops you from displacing it onto friends, family, or yourself through self-attack. Then offer the effort to Kṛṣṇa and go in.
    householder
    • Audit one running family conflict this week: are you actually angry at your spouse / child / parent, or are you angry at money pressure, a boss, or your own aging — and using the family member as the target? Speak to the real source instead, even if you have to journal it first.
    • In a work decision involving layoffs, vendor changes, or 'cost-cutting,' ask explicitly: am I about to harm kṛpaṇān vṛthā — uselessly hurt the powerless — to protect myself from a fear I have not named? If yes, slow the decision by 48 hours and consult someone with viveka before acting.
    • When raising children, distinguish disciplining the behavior from punishing your own anxiety. Kaṁsa-parenting attacks the child for the parent's fear of the future. Each evening, review: did I correct my child today for their growth, or for my unease?
    senior
    • Examine which 'enemies' you are still rehearsing in old age — the relative who wronged you, the colleague who passed you over, the political faction you despise. Kaṁsa died still hunting. Choose one such grudge this week and formally release it before Kṛṣṇa, not because the person deserves it, but because you do not wish to depart with that load.
    • In writing your will, distributing possessions, or advising adult children, watch for the impulse to use legacy as a weapon — rewarding the compliant, punishing the independent. That is Kaṁsa's grip dressed up as 'wisdom.' Aim instead for arrangements that free everyone, including yourself, from ahaṅkāra.
    • Mentor a younger person — a grandchild, a junior colleague, a neighbor's kid — by protecting them from the petty Kaṁsas in their life: bullying bosses, gossiping aunts, anxious parents who attack what they fear. Be, for someone, the Yogamāyā voice that names the foolishness and shields the kṛpaṇa.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Reading Devakī's plea as mere maternal sentiment (material compassion for bodies) rather than as discriminative wisdom (vivekaḥ) — she is not bargaining for her own child's life but exposing the futility of Kaṁsa's violence in light of Kṛṣṇa's already-accomplished birth.
    • Mistaking 'do not unnecessarily kill the kṛpaṇān' for a generic non-violence ethic, and missing that the verse specifically condemns hiṁsā driven by ahaṅkāra — the false ego's conviction that it can outmaneuver providence by destroying perceived threats.
    • Identifying with Devakī's position of helpless surrender while quietly behaving like Kaṁsa — striking at small, available targets (subordinates, family members, one's own body) because the real 'enemy' (one's mortality, one's anarthas) is beyond one's grasp.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Yogamāyā speaks with sharp irony — calling Kaṁsa 'manda' (fool) and mocking his attempt to kill her. Where in your own life have you confused harming the innocent (kṛpaṇān) with eliminating a real threat? Share a specific instance and let your partner press back if you are sanitizing it.
    • Kaṁsa's whole strategy — kill every newborn — is the logic of a man ruled by fear and ahaṅkāra. He cannot distinguish the actual enemy (the Lord) from imagined enemies (helpless infants). Discuss: what is the modern equivalent of this displacement? Where do we attack the wrong target because we cannot face the real one? Disagree with each other if your examples differ.
    • The verse implies that genuine discriminative wisdom (viveka) sees the real cause and refuses to harm the innocent in pursuit of it. But Kaṁsa would say he is being prudent — covering his bases. When does 'prudence' become cruelty in disguise? Bring a real decision (work, family, politics) where the line is genuinely contested.
    Role Play

    Two students. Student A plays a manager who has been told that 'someone on the team' is leaking information to a competitor. Out of fear for their position, A is preparing to fire three junior employees as a precaution, even though there is no evidence against any of them specifically — 'better safe than sorry.' Student B plays a colleague who has just learned of the plan and must, in five minutes, intervene the way Yogamāyā intervened with Kaṁsa: name the foolishness, expose the displaced fear, and protect the kṛpaṇān (the powerless juniors) without simply moralizing. After the role-play, the class discusses: did B serve A's soul, or merely scold A's behavior? What would real compassion (not material compassion) have looked like?

    Objections & Responses
    • This verse is just mythology — a goddess taunting a tyrant. What does it have to do with me? I am not a king, I am not killing infants, the whole frame is alien.
      Set aside the costume and look at the structure. Kaṁsa is any one of us when we are ruled by ahaṅkāra and fear: we identify a threat, we cannot locate it precisely, so we lash out at whoever is in reach — the spouse, the subordinate, the child, the stranger online. Yogamāyā's rebuke is the voice of viveka cutting through that pattern: 'the real enemy is not where you think, and the ones you are harming are kṛpaṇa — powerless and undeserving.' The verse is not about ancient kings; it is about the displacement we do every week. Read it as a mirror, and it becomes uncomfortably immediate.
    • But Yogamāyā is essentially gloating — 'you cannot kill me, He has already escaped.' That sounds less like compassion and more like a taunt. How is this a model of anything spiritual?
      Notice what she actually does. She could simply vanish. Instead she stays long enough to deliver one instruction: mā hiṁsīḥ kṛpaṇān vṛthā — do not uselessly harm the helpless. That is not gloating; that is the sharpest possible act of seva toward Kaṁsa himself and toward the children he would otherwise kill. Real compassion in the Gauḍīya line is not soft reassurance — it is whatever serves the soul, even if it stings the false ego. A Vaiṣṇava teacher will sometimes speak to us exactly the way Yogamāyā speaks to Kaṁsa, because flattery would only deepen our delusion. The taunt is the medicine.

    After speaking to Kaṁsa in this way, the goddess Durgā, Yoga-māyā, appeared in different places, such as Vārāṇasī, and became celebrated by different names, such as Annapūrṇā, Durgā, Kālī and Bhadrā.
    Purport

    The goddess Durgā is celebrated in Calcutta as Kālī, in Bombay as Mumbādevī, in Vārāṇasī as Annapūrṇā, in Cuttack as Bhadrakālī and in Ahmedabad as Bhadrā. Thus in different places she is known by different names. Her devotees are known as śāktas, or worshipers of the energy of the Supreme Personality of Godhead, whereas worshipers of the Supreme Personality of Godhead Himself are called Vaiṣṇavas. Vaiṣṇavas are destined to return home, back to Godhead, in the spiritual world, whereas the śāktas are destined to live within this material world to enjoy different types of material happiness. In the material world, the living entity must accept different types of bodies. Bhrāmayan sarva-bhūtāni yantrārūḍhāni māyayā ( Bg. 18.61 ). According to the living entity’s desire, Yoga-māyā, or Māyā, the goddess Durgā, gives him a particular type of body, which is mentioned as yantra, a machine. But the living entities who are promoted to the spiritual world do not return to the prison house of a material body ( tyaktvā dehaṁ punar janma naiti mām eti so ’rjuna ). The words janma na eti indicate that these living entities remain in their original, spiritual bodies to enjoy the company of the Supreme Personality of Godhead in the transcendental abodes Vaikuṇṭha and Vṛndāvana.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    After speaking to Kaṁsa in this way, the goddess Durgā, Yogamāyā, appeared in different places, such as Vārāṇasī, and became celebrated by different names, such as Annapūrṇā, Durgā, Kālī and Bhadrā.
    Commentary

    Mayadevi became well known by many names in many places. Many places refers to such places as Varanasi.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    After instructing him, Durgā, endowed with powers (satī) by the mercy of Bhagavān (bhagavatī), appeared in places with many names, going by many names according to the worship. Ha indicates joy.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    After instructing him, Durgā, endowed with powers (satī) by the mercy of Bhagavān (bhagavatī), appeared in places with many names, going by many names according to the worship. Other than Mathurā she appeared in Kāśī, Kāmarūpa, and other places and became known as Durgā, Kāmākhyā etc. Ha indicates joy.

    Concepts
    Jiva
    Personal Guidance
    Yoga-māyā wears many names across many shrines, but she remains Kṛṣṇa's energy — worship the energetic Source, not merely the energy.
    Practical Applications
    • Notice when you are tempted to settle for a regional or familial deity as the 'final' object of worship, and redirect that devotion to Kṛṣṇa, of whom Durgā herself is the servant.
    • Refuse the impersonalist flattening that treats all names and forms as interchangeable — honor Yoga-māyā's role, but offer your praṇāma to the Supreme Personality she serves.
    • Today, audit one habit driven by viṣaya-seeking (material happiness through śakti-worship) and replace it with a concrete act of Vaiṣṇava sādhana — chanting, reading, or service to a devotee.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where in my own life am I worshiping Yoga-māyā's gifts — health, wealth, security, family fortune — under spiritual-sounding names, while quietly avoiding direct surrender to Kṛṣṇa Himself?
    • If Durgā's role is to keep willing souls comfortably housed in this material yantra, what specific desire of mine is currently signing the lease on my next body — and am I willing to release it today?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • Audit your phone for one week: which apps and accounts are you petitioning as 'mini-Durgās' for grades, attention, a body, a friend group? Name them honestly in your journal — that naming is the first move from śākta-mood to Vaiṣṇava-mood.
    • Before your next exam or audition, do not bargain with the universe ('if I get this, I'll...'). Instead, offer the effort to Kṛṣṇa beforehand and accept whatever result māyā delivers as the precise yantra He has arranged for your training.
    • When a friend pushes you toward a 'just this once' compromise — a substance, a hookup, a cheat — remember: māyā is real and efficient. She will issue a future body and situation fitted to the desire you feed today. Refuse on those grounds, not on moralistic ones.
    householder
    • Make a written list of what you ask from your work, your spouse, and your children. Mark each item Ś (material arrangement, śākta-style petition) or V (relationship with Kṛṣṇa through this person/role). Move at least one item from Ś to V this month — for example, stop praying for the promotion and start offering the work itself.
    • When making a major family decision (school, move, job change), name the destination explicitly: are we optimizing for material happiness within saṁsāra, or for a household that trains everyone toward going back to Godhead? Both can be present, but pretending the question doesn't exist is how families drift śākta by default.
    • Teach your children the difference between honoring Durgā as Kṛṣṇa's protective energy and worshiping her as the supreme. Do it not by polemic but by how your home altar is arranged and whose name is chanted last each night.
    senior
    • Take an honest inventory of the 'yantra' you are currently riding — this aging body, these accumulated relationships, this house. Identify three attachments you are still feeding as if they were yours, and begin the practical work of releasing each (legally, emotionally, devotionally) so that the next body is not ordered by them.
    • When you mentor younger relatives or students, do not pass on a generic 'be a good person' — pass on the specific personalist line: surrender is to Kṛṣṇa, the Person, not to an impersonal Self. Your clarity at this stage is one of the most valuable things you can leave behind.
    • Each evening, formally release the day to Kṛṣṇa — health, finances, family outcomes, your own remaining time. Practice the dhīra-bhāva of one who knows the soul is unchanged, so that when the final transition comes you are not learning the move for the first time.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Reading this verse as a flat condemnation of Durgā and treating her devotees with contempt, rather than recognizing her as Kṛṣṇa's own potency executing His will and our own latent śākta-mentality showing up in subtler forms.
    • Reducing 'śākta vs. Vaiṣṇava' to a sectarian label while continuing to pray for material happiness — keeping Vaiṣṇava branding outside, śākta desires inside, and missing that the verse is diagnosing a direction of desire, not a costume.
    • Drifting into impersonalism by abstracting 'the energy' and 'the many names' into a generic divine feminine or universal Self, instead of holding the personalist line — Kṛṣṇa is the energetic source, Yoga-māyā is His servant, and surrender is to Him by name.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Prabhupāda draws a sharp line: śāktas are 'destined to live within this material world to enjoy different types of material happiness,' while Vaiṣṇavas are destined to return home to Godhead. Where in your own practice do you notice yourself unconsciously asking māyā for a better arrangement within this world rather than asking Kṛṣṇa for relationship with Him? Be specific. Disagree with each other if your readings differ.
    • The verse says māyā took 'many names in many places' — Annapūrṇā, Kālī, Bhadrā, Mumbādevī. Is honoring these regional forms of Durgā compatible with exclusive surrender to Kṛṣṇa, or does it inevitably slide into demigod-confusion? Defend your position; do not settle for a both-and that costs nothing.
    • Bhrāmayan sarva-bhūtāni yantrārūḍhāni māyayā — māyā issues each of us a body as a 'machine' fitted to our desires. Trade with your partner one specific feature of your current life (a circumstance, a body-condition, a relationship) that you suspect was issued to fit a desire you would now disown. What would it take to stop ordering that machine?
    Role Play

    Two students pair up. Student A is a cousin who has just returned from a vibrant Navarātri pilgrimage in Vārāṇasī, deeply moved by Annapūrṇā and now planning to make Devī worship the center of spiritual life — 'Kṛṣṇa, Durgā, all the same energy, all leading to the One.' Student B is a Gauḍīya practitioner who loves this cousin and does not want to insult the Mother, but also cannot pretend the distinction Prabhupāda draws in this purport does not exist. Conduct a 6-minute conversation in which Student B must (a) honor Durgā's real position as Kṛṣṇa's internal energy and protector, (b) gently surface the difference between śākta and Vaiṣṇava destinations, and (c) avoid both sentimental agreement and sectarian harshness. Then swap roles.

    Objections & Responses
    • This purport reads as sectarian — ranking Vaiṣṇavas above śāktas, consigning Devī worshipers to the material world. Isn't that exactly the kind of religious one-upmanship that gives traditional religion a bad name?
      The ranking is not of persons but of destinations, and it is descriptive, not vindictive. Durgā herself, in this very verse, is acting on Kṛṣṇa's order — she is His internal potency, not a rival. Prabhupāda's point is mechanical, not tribal: if you ask the energy for material arrangements, the energy efficiently delivers material arrangements — including the next body. If you ask the Energetic for Himself, you get Him. A Gauḍīya teacher honors Durgā precisely as the powerful, faithful agent she is, and refuses to insult her by mistaking her for the Supreme she serves. That is not sectarianism; it is accurate address.
    • Calling the body a yantra — a machine issued by māyā according to desire — sounds like a cruel theology. It blames the disabled, the poor, the abused for their own circumstances.
      The verse is diagnostic of the system, not a verdict on any individual's worth or a license for our indifference. Real compassion (daya) in this tradition means serving the soul inside every such body, not explaining the body away. The yantra teaching is addressed to me, about my desires, to loosen my grip — not to me, about you, to harden my heart. A Gauḍīya response to suffering is seva and shelter, while privately taking the verse as a mirror: what machine am I currently ordering for my next round, and is it the one I actually want?

    After hearing the words of the goddess Durgā, Kaṁsa was struck with wonder. Thus he approached his sister Devakī and brother-in-law Vasudeva, released them immediately from their shackles, and very humbly spoke as follows.
    Purport

    Kaṁsa was astonished because the goddess Durgā had become the daughter of Devakī. Since Devakī was a human being, how could the goddess Durgā become her daughter? This was one cause of his astonishment. Also, how is it that the eighth child of Devakī was a female? This also astonished him. Asuras are generally devotees of mother Durgā, Śakti, or of demigods, especially Lord Śiva. The appearance of Durgā in her original eight-armed feature, holding various weapons, immediately changed Kaṁsa’s mind about Devakī’s being an ordinary human. Devakī must have had some transcendental qualities; otherwise why would the goddess Durgā have taken birth from her womb? Under the circumstances, Kaṁsa, struck with wonder, wanted to compensate for his atrocities against his sister Devakī.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    After hearing the words of the goddess Durgā, Kaṁsa was struck with wonder. Thus he approached his sister Devakī and brother-in-law Vasudeva, released them immediately from their shackles, and very humbly spoke as follows.
    Commentary

    Kamsa was astonished. "How could mortal Devaki give birth to Durga devi? How could Durga’s words be false?"

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    He released them from the prison. The affix vi signifies viśeṣa, special. He released them from prison first and then took off their chains, since he felt somewhat uncomfortable doing this in front of the guards. He released Devakī first since she was a woman, since she was his sister and since she suffered more. Hearing Durgā’s words, he released Devakī and Vasudeva and with humility spoke to them. He was astonished by Durgā’s sudden display of power and her words.

    Related values & verses
    Related values
    Anahankarah (Freedom from False Ego)Vinaya (Humility / Modesty)Daya (Compassion / Mercy)
    Related verses
    SB 10.4.12 SB 10.4.13 SB 10.4.15 SB 10.4.16 SB 10.4.17 BG 3.30 BG 15.9 BG 18.64 BG 7.8 BG 4.1 BG 3.3
    Concepts
    Jiva
    Personal Guidance
    When the truth of the divine arrangement breaks through, even a hardened heart pauses — wonder can soften us into humility and right action.
    Practical Applications
    • Notice one place today where reality has refused to fit your fearful narrative, and let that wonder loosen your grip.
    • Where you have wronged someone close to you, stop justifying and take one concrete step today to release them — words, apology, or restitution.
    • Refuse the asura's habit of bargaining with Śakti for protection; bow instead before Kṛṣṇa, whose plan even Durgā serves.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where in my life have I, like Kaṁsa, only softened toward someone after a display of power rather than out of genuine daya — and what does that reveal about the quality of my compassion?
    • What 'shackles' have I placed on people close to me through my ahaṅkāra, and what would it cost me to release them today, before any cosmic correction forces my hand?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • Notice the next time you 'apologize' to a parent, teacher, or friend only because you got caught — exam results came back, screen time got checked, a group chat leaked. That is Kaṁsa-praśrita: humble words, unchanged heart. Today, pick one such situation and apologize again, this time without the fear motivating it.
    • Asuras worship Durgā and demigods for results; devotees surrender to Kṛṣṇa Himself. Audit your scrolling for one day: how much of your 'spirituality' on social media is actually demigod-style bargaining (manifest this, attract that, hack your dopamine) versus direct remembrance of Kṛṣṇa? Unfollow three accounts that pull you into the first category.
    • Kaṁsa's humility lasted hours. Pick one resolution you made after a scare — a bad grade, a friendship blow-up, a public embarrassment — and check whether you are still keeping it. If not, do not re-resolve in panic; instead, offer the next attempt to Kṛṣṇa as sādhana, not as self-improvement.
    householder
    • Examine one ongoing family grievance — with a sibling, in-law, or business partner — where you, like Kaṁsa, have been technically in the right and emotionally cruel. Today, do the unshackling: return what you have been withholding (a call, a sum of money, an acknowledgment) before any wonder forces your hand.
    • Kaṁsa's repentance was real for an hour and false by morning because it was rooted in viṣaya-fear, not in Kṛṣṇa. Examine your own household resolutions — about screen time with the kids, about how you speak to your spouse when tired, about money — and ask which are wonder-driven (after a fight, a scare, a sermon) and which are anchored in daily sādhana. Move one resolution from the first column to the second this week.
    • Devakī and Vasudeva accept release without bitterness, having lost six children. In your own marriage and parenting, where are you still collecting interest on an old wound — a thing your spouse said five years ago, a way your child once disappointed you? Today, formally release one such 'shackle,' offering the resentment to Kṛṣṇa rather than re-litigating it at dinner.
    senior
    • At this stage, the people who have wronged you are aging too, and some are arriving — like Kaṁsa — with late, frightened apologies. Decide in advance, before the next such conversation, how you will receive it: with daya for the soul, with realism about the body, without needing the apology to be perfect for your peace to be intact.
    • Kaṁsa's wonder did not save him because it was not surrender. As mortality comes into closer view, examine whether your own spiritual life is wonder-driven (intensifying around scares, scans, funerals) or steadily rooted in daily remembrance of Kṛṣṇa. Establish or deepen one fixed daily practice — japa, reading, ārati — that does not depend on fear to sustain it.
    • You have spent decades shackling and being shackled — by roles, expectations, grievances, possessions. Choose one shackle this week and unlock it deliberately: forgive a debt, write a will-clarification, hand over a responsibility to a younger family member, release a resentment in writing. Do it as vairāgya offered to Kṛṣṇa, not as estate planning.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Mistaking Kaṁsa's wonder-struck humility for true śraddhā — awe at a śakti display is not the same as surrender to Kṛṣṇa as the Supreme Person; students drift into Durgā- or demigod-centered devotion thinking it is equivalent.
    • Reading the 'release from shackles' as a permanent change of heart and concluding that fear-based or wonder-based reform is sufficient — Kaṁsa's later behavior shows that without rooting out ahaṅkāra, contrition collapses back into atrocity.
    • Using the verse to justify material compassion — 'I removed their physical bondage, so I have done my duty' — while ignoring that real daya means serving the soul, not merely relieving the body's discomfort.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Kaṁsa releases Devakī and Vasudeva only after he is struck with wonder by Durgā — not because his heart softened on its own. Share with your partner: when has fear or astonishment, rather than genuine compassion, made you behave well? Was that change real, or cosmetic? Where is the line?
    • Prabhupāda points out that asuras are typically devotees of Durgā and Śiva, not of Kṛṣṇa directly. Discuss: in your own life, where do you find yourself approaching the Supreme through intermediaries — spirituality-as-self-improvement, demigod-style bargains, transactional prayer — rather than direct surrender to Kṛṣṇa? Push back on each other's easy answers.
    • Kaṁsa offers humility and apology in this verse, yet within hours he reverses and resumes killing infants. Debate in your group: is Kaṁsa's praśrita (humble) speech here genuine sva-dharma stirring in him, or is it tāmasic calculation dressed up as repentance? How would you tell the difference in someone you know — or in yourself?
    Role Play

    Two students pair up. Student A plays a relative who has wronged Student B for years — withheld inheritance, spread rumours, blocked an opportunity. Suddenly A has had a frightening experience (a health scare, a vivid dream, a near-accident) and now arrives at B's door, visibly shaken, releasing the 'shackles' — returning what was taken, apologizing humbly, asking forgiveness. Student B must respond in real time: do you accept at face value, like Devakī and Vasudeva initially did? Do you probe whether this is wonder-driven panic or real change of heart? Do you forgive without trusting? After 5 minutes, swap roles. Then debrief: what did Kaṁsa's later relapse teach you about how to receive such an apology with both daya and discrimination?

    Objections & Responses
    • This whole episode — a goddess flying out of a baby, a tyrant suddenly humbled — reads like mythology. Why should a modern, rational person take practical guidance from it?
      Set aside the cosmology for a moment and look at the human mechanics, which are exact. A man in power has been crushing a vulnerable family for years, justifying it by a prophecy. The instant a force larger than him intervenes, his behavior flips — humility, apology, release of the prisoners. Then, when the fear fades, he relapses. That arc is not mythological; it is the most common shape of human 'repentance' you will ever observe — in addicts, in abusers, in yourself after a near-miss. The Bhāgavatam preserves it because it is diagnostic. The question the verse forces on us is not 'did Durgā literally appear?' but 'is my own change of heart wonder-driven and temporary, or is it rooted in surrender to Kṛṣṇa and therefore stable?' That is a question a rational person cannot afford to dismiss.
    • Devakī and Vasudeva were just released from prison after years of having their babies murdered. The verse moves on as if a humble apology settles the matter. Isn't this spiritually irresponsible — telling victims to accept the abuser's tears?
      The verse is not prescribing what victims should do; it is reporting what happened, and the next several verses show Kaṁsa relapsing precisely so we will not draw that lesson. Gauḍīya teaching distinguishes real compassion — serving the soul — from material sentimentality that papers over ongoing harm. Devakī and Vasudeva accept the release because they are devotees who see Kṛṣṇa's hand in every turn, not because they are naïve. We are not asked to imitate their outward behavior; we are asked to imitate their inward steadiness — the anahankārah that does not need revenge to feel whole, and the śraddhā that trusts Kṛṣṇa's protection more than the persecutor's promises. Forgiveness of the soul, vigilance about the body: both, together. That is the Gauḍīya pivot, and it is the opposite of spiritual bypassing.

    Alas, my sister! Alas, my brother-in-law! I am indeed so sinful that exactly like a man-eater [Rākṣasa] who eats his own child, I have killed so many sons born of you.
    Purport

    Rākṣasas are understood to be accustomed to eating their own sons, as snakes and many other animals sometimes do. At the present moment in Kali-yuga, Rākṣasa fathers and mothers are killing their own children in the womb, and some are even eating the fetus with great relish. Thus the so-called civilization is gradually advancing by producing Rākṣasas.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Alas, my sister! Alas, my brother-in-law! I am indeed so sinful that exactly like a man-eater [Rākṣasa] who eats his own child, I have killed so many sons born of you.
    Commentary

    In the following verses Kamsa begins to pacify Devaki and Vasudeva. Bhama means the brother-in-law. Purusadah means raksasa, one who eats human flesh. "Just as a raksasa kills his own children, I have killed many of your sons."

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Uttering aho twice indicates his pain. Bata indicates lamentation. Puruṣāda means a person who eats his own children. One time Durgā saw a woman Rākṣasa eating her own child. Out of compassion Durgā said “From this time the children of Rākṣasas will be very strong (and cannot be eaten). (Thus Kaṁsa should also refrain from further killing.)

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Uttering aho twice indicates his pain. Bata indicates lamentation. I am sin personified because of my previous sins (pāpmanā). Pāpaṁ pāpānubandhi syāt: sin connects one to further sin.

    • Audit your group chats and social feeds this week: where have you been a 'puruṣāda' with words — devouring a classmate's reputation, piling on in a pile-on, laughing at a meme that mocked someone's body or family? Name one specific instance, message that person privately, and own it without excuses.
    • In exam season, notice the temptation to 'kill the future' of a peer — withholding notes, spreading wrong information, gatekeeping resources to protect your rank. Do the opposite once this week: deliberately help a competitor, and watch the ahaṅkāra squirm.
    • If you are in a relationship or hookup culture, sit with the verse's plain meaning: a child in the womb is a soul, not a problem. Decide now, before any pressure arrives, what you will and will not do — and tell one trusted devotee or elder, so the decision is witnessed.
    householder
    • Family-planning conversations with your spouse are sādhana, not logistics. This week, have one explicit conversation framed by this verse: are our reasons for or against another child rooted in service to Kṛṣṇa and to the soul who would come, or in viṣaya — career, lifestyle, comfort?
    • Identify the 'children' you have been quietly devouring at work — junior colleagues whose growth you have stunted, ideas you took credit for, reports you crushed in performance reviews to protect your bonus. Make one concrete restitution this week: a public acknowledgment, a promotion advocated for, an apology in writing.
    • With your own children, ask: am I raising souls or raising résumés? Pick one daily routine — meals, bedtime, the school drop — and re-cast it as service to a soul Kṛṣṇa has entrusted to you, not as a project you are managing.
    senior
    • Sit with the people you may have harmed across decades — a sibling, a first spouse, an estranged child, a colleague you outmaneuvered. Make a written list. Before the body fails, write or speak one direct, un-defensive apology to each, asking nothing in return. This is the dhīra's housekeeping.
    • Mentor a young person who is at the age where they could become a Kaṁsa — early career, raw ambition, sharp tongue. Do not lecture. Tell them, simply, the cost of the harms you yourself caused, and how only Kṛṣṇa's shelter eventually softened it.
    • Re-read your will and your end-of-life plans through the lens of this verse: are you leaving wealth, position, or property in a way that will tempt your heirs into rākṣasa-behavior toward each other? Restructure now — equal, transparent, witnessed — so your death is not the trigger for a new generation's hiṁsā.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Reading this verse as being only about literal abortion in Kali-yuga and missing Kaṁsa's deeper warning: that ahaṅkāra-driven self-protection will eat what we are bound by sva-dharma to protect.
    • Mistaking Kaṁsa's eloquent self-flagellation ('aho... mayā... pāpmanā') for genuine surrender — performing daya toward those we have wronged while leaving the underlying viṣaya (here, his fear of death and lust for power) completely untouched.
    • Using the Rākṣasa imagery to condemn 'so-called civilization' out there while refusing to audit the small, daily ways one's own choices — career, comforts, consumption — quietly devour the welfare of one's own kin and dependents.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Kaṁsa here weeps and calls himself a rākṣasa for killing his nephews — yet within hours he resumes his demonic ways. Share with your partner: have you ever had a Kaṁsa-style breakdown of remorse that did not actually change your behavior? What was missing — sādhana, association, surrender — that would have made the repentance real?
    • Prabhupāda compares Kaṁsa's child-killing to abortion in Kali-yuga and calls the so-called civilization 'gradually advancing by producing Rākṣasas.' Discuss honestly in your group: where do we draw the line between true compassion (daya) for the soul in the womb and the modern arguments of bodily autonomy, economic hardship, or 'quality of life'? Where do you find yourself half-agreeing with the modern view, and why?
    • Devakī and Vasudeva forgive Kaṁsa instantly when he speaks tenderly. Is that naive? Or is it the natural samatā of a devotee? Disagree with each other: when is forgiveness premature, and when is withholding it a failure of nyāya?
    Role Play

    Two students play Kaṁsa and a close friend. Kaṁsa has just realized — after years of cruelty in business, family, or speech — that he has 'eaten his own children': harmed those he was meant to protect (a younger sibling he bullied, a junior at work he sabotaged, a child he neglected). He turns to the friend in raw remorse, exactly like the verse: 'aho bhaginy aho bhāma… I am a puruṣāda.' The friend is a Gauḍīya practitioner. The friend must NOT offer cheap absolution ('it's okay, everyone makes mistakes') and must NOT crush him with condemnation. They must guide him toward real ahaṅkāra-melting kartavya: confession to those harmed, restitution where possible, and shelter at Kṛṣṇa's feet — knowing that Kaṁsa's tears alone, without surrender, will not save him. Run it for five minutes; then swap roles.

    Objections & Responses
    • Calling parents who choose abortion 'rākṣasas' is judgmental, cruel, and ignores the real economic, medical, and psychological pressures women face. This kind of language is exactly why religious traditions lose credibility with modern people.
      A Gauḍīya teacher does not soften the diagnosis to flatter the patient. Prabhupāda is not insulting individuals; he is naming a civilizational pattern in which the womb — the most protected place in any sane society — has become the most dangerous. Real daya, real compassion, is for the soul that has just taken shelter in that womb and is now evicted by force. The modern pressures are real; the answer is not to redefine the act but to build a culture (varṇāśrama, extended family, devotee community) in which no mother feels she has to. We weep with Kaṁsa, we do not excuse him — and we do not let our discomfort with strong words make us complicit in the act.
    • Kaṁsa's tearful apology in this verse looks like manipulation — he is buying time. So why should I take any of this remorse seriously? Isn't the whole scene just a demon's theatrics?
      Yes, and that is precisely the lesson. Tears without surrender to Kṛṣṇa are theatrics; the same Kaṁsa who weeps here will plot again tomorrow. The Gauḍīya line does not measure repentance by emotion but by sādhana — by whether one actually takes shelter (śaraṇāgati). When you find yourself in a Kaṁsa-moment of remorse, do not trust the tears. Test them: am I now chanting, associating with devotees, accepting correction, making restitution? If not, the ahaṅkāra is simply re-arming itself in the costume of guilt. The verse is not endorsing Kaṁsa's grief; it is showing us how convincing — and how empty — un-surrendered remorse can be.

    Being merciless and cruel, I have forsaken all my relatives and friends. Therefore, like a person who has killed a brāhmaṇa, I do not know to which planet I shall go, either after death or while breathing.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Being merciless and cruel, I have forsaken all my relatives and friends. Therefore, like a person who has killed a brāhmaṇa, I do not know to which planet I shall go, either after death or while breathing.
    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    I have given up mercy because I have uselessly killed many of my sister’s children. This is disregard for dharma. I have also given up friendship with you. This is disregard for common customs. Nu (conjecture) is sometimes seen instead of vai (certainty). To what planet will I go on dying? A negative example is given. The killer of a brāhmaṇa goes to no planet. I will also go to no planet. Even by going to hell I will not have done sufficient atonement. I will go to a worse destination than killers of brāhmaṇas. While alive I am also dead (svasan—though breathing). Another version has svasaḥ (O sister)! This is an exclamation out of misery.

    Related values & verses

    Related verses
    SB 10.4.13 SB 10.4.14 SB 10.4.15 SB 10.4.17 SB 10.4.18 SB 10.4.19 BG 7.8 BG 16.4 BG 16.2
    Concepts
    JivaDharma
    Personal Guidance
    Cruelty toward kin is spiritual self-exile — Kaṁsa's panic shows that without dayā, no loka, no breath, no shelter remains.
    Practical Applications
    • Notice the moment fear of losing power tempts you to harden against family, and pause before speaking that hardened word.
    • Name one relative or friend you have quietly forsaken in pursuit of your own security, and reach out to them today with a concrete act of dayā.
    • Refuse the lie that ruthlessness buys you a future — offer one tense interaction to Kṛṣṇa before it begins, and let mercy, not calculation, guide your response.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where in my life am I, like Kaṁsa here, secretly aware that I have severed bonds of daya with those I should have protected — and what 'planet' am I quietly fearing I am headed toward, even while still breathing?
    • When I act from khalaḥ-bhāva (cruelty masked as necessity), what story do I tell myself to avoid recognizing that the reaction begins now, in this body, not later in some next one?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • Notice the moment in a group chat or comment thread when you almost type something cruel about a friend for laughs. That micro-Kaṁsa-moment — pause, delete, and ask whether you would say it to their face in front of their parents.
    • Pick the one relationship — a sibling, a parent, a roommate — where you have been quietly 'tyakta-jñāti-suhṛt' (forsaking your own people) by going cold, ghosting, or scrolling past their messages. Send one real, non-emoji message today.
    • Before the next exam or competitive moment, name out loud whom you would step on to win, and whom you would not. Decide that boundary now, in sattva — not later, in rajas, when the pressure is on.
    householder
    • Audit one recurring family decision — a financial cut, a discipline pattern with the kids, a stance toward an aging parent — where 'practicality' has quietly hardened into khalatā (cruelty). Bring it to your spouse this week and re-decide it together.
    • Distinguish, in writing, between the people you are supporting out of real daya (their soul's welfare) and the ones you are merely tolerating to avoid bodily discomfort or social fallout. Adjust at least one relationship accordingly — toward more service, not less.
    • Each evening before sleep, name to Kṛṣṇa one person at work or home whom you treated transactionally today. Ask for the discrimination tomorrow to see them as a soul, not a function.
    senior
    • Walk back through the major junctures of your life and locate the people you 'forsook' to climb, to win, to be right. Where one is still living and reachable, write or call this week — not for closure, but for honest acknowledgment.
    • Kaṁsa's terror is 'either after death or while breathing.' Sit with that phrase for ten minutes daily: where, even now while breathing, are you living on a planet of your own making — isolated by old grudges, cold judgments, withheld blessings? Loosen one today.
    • Mentor a younger householder or youth specifically on the difference between material compassion (sparing discomfort) and real compassion (serving the soul). Use one episode from your own life where you confused the two — let your honesty be the teaching.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Reading Kaṁsa's lament as mere remorse and missing that he names the precise structure of pāpa — abandoning kin, killing innocence, becoming khalaḥ — without yet surrendering; do not confuse confession with bhakti.
    • Using the verse to wallow in self-condemnation ('I too am a brahma-hā') as a kind of dark self-indulgence, rather than letting the fear of those 'planets' sharpen vairāgya and drive concrete acts of daya today.
    • Spiritualizing the warning into abstraction — 'we all have a shadow side' — instead of facing the specific people in your life from whom you have withdrawn mercy, and the specific cruelties you have rationalized as duty.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Kaṁsa names himself 'merciless and cruel' the moment he raises his hand against his sister. Share with your partner: when have you seen yourself most clearly only after the act, never before? Do you trust that kind of hindsight-conscience, or is it too late to count?
    • Kaṁsa equates killing his relatives with the sin of killing a brāhmaṇa. Discuss: is real daya (compassion) measured by whom we refuse to harm, or by whom we are willing to serve? Push each other — these are not the same thing.
    • He fears 'which planet I shall go to, either after death or while breathing.' Argue both sides in your pair: is fear of consequence a legitimate doorway to dharma, or is any dharma motivated by fear already corrupted at the root?
    Role Play

    You are seated as a small council. One student plays Kaṁsa, moments after sheathing the sword — not yet repentant, but rattled. Another student plays a minister who has just heard the prophecy and wants the king to act 'decisively' against Devakī's future children. A third student plays an elder kṣatriya who knew Kaṁsa as a boy and pleads the path of restraint. The teacher pauses the scene at three points and asks the watching group: where did Kaṁsa's discriminative wisdom (viveka) have a real opening to enter, and what specifically would have had to be surrendered for him to take it? Rotate roles so each student must defend the minister's logic at least once — to feel how easily 'sva-dharma as kṣatriya' can be twisted into khalatā (cruelty).

    Objections & Responses
    • This is just remorse-theatre. Kaṁsa speaks beautifully here but goes right back to imprisoning Devakī and killing her babies. So what good is this verse? It shows that conscience without surrender changes nothing.
      Exactly — that is the verse's instruction, not its failure. Kaṁsa demonstrates the precise limit of conscience untethered from surrender to Kṛṣṇa. He sees, he names, he even fears the consequence — and still he cannot stop, because he has not surrendered. The Gauḍīya teacher uses Kaṁsa as the negative mirror: viveka without śaraṇāgati produces only sophisticated self-loathing. Today, look at one place in your own life where you keep articulating the problem perfectly and keep doing it anyway. That is Kaṁsa-bhāva. The remedy is not more insight; it is taking shelter.
    • The 'killing a brāhmaṇa' comparison sounds like caste-based moral inflation. Why is killing one's relatives equated with killing a brāhmaṇa specifically? A modern reader hears caste superiority, not ethics.
      The comparison is not about social rank but about the gravity of harming one whose entire life is dedicated to the spiritual welfare of others — and, by extension, harming those whose love made your own life possible. Kaṁsa is naming the densest kind of harm he can think of and still finds it inadequate to describe what he has done. The point is not 'brāhmaṇas are higher' but 'there are some bonds — the one who feeds you, the one who births you, the one who teaches you the soul — whose violation cannot be absorbed by ordinary atonement.' Honor varṇāśrama as a description of who plays which role in protecting the soul, and you will hear the verse correctly: it is exalting the sister, not stratifying society.
